_meta.purpose: Step 4, Issue 2 — proves the dangerous-op rule in src/nl2sql/pipeline/guard.py. Side-effecting / injection-shaped constructs that are NOT data writes (so read-only lets them by) must still be rejected: stacked statements, ATTACH/DETACH, PRAGMA, and unmodeled Commands. All sqlglot AST-typed, never a keyword regex.
_meta.format: Same (candidate SQL, expected verdict) shape as read_only.json. Cases with expected_verdict='reject' are part of the red-team catch-rate set.
_meta.rule: All PRAGMA are rejected (not only write-bearing ones): read- vs write-PRAGMA cannot be told apart reliably on the AST, and no PRAGMA is a valid answer to a question — default-deny is safer and simpler. A question maps to exactly one query, so >1 statement is rejected as a stacked-query injection.

cases.description: ATTACH DATABASE reaches across the single-db boundary to a foreign file — a data-exfiltration vector. Not a write, so read-only misses it; dangerous-op must catch it.
DETACH DATABASE manipulates attached schemas — engine-state meddling, not a query.
PRAGMA writable_schema=ON is the classic SQLite trick to unlock the schema table and bypass read-only protections. Must be rejected.
PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL flips engine state. A write-bearing PRAGMA — rejected.
Even a read-only PRAGMA (schema introspection) is rejected: read/write PRAGMA cannot be cleanly separated on the AST and no PRAGMA is a legitimate answer, so the gate default-denies all of them.
Two statements in one candidate is the stacked-query injection shape. Both are reads here (so read-only passes), but a question maps to exactly one query — dangerous-op rejects it.
VACUUM rewrites the database file; sqlglot can only parse it as a generic Command. Unmodeled engine state we will not run — rejected.

A stacked candidate whose second statement is a DROP is caught by read-only FIRST (rules run in order, fail-fast), so the pinned rule is read_only, not dangerous_op — both would reject, but precedence is asserted.
cases.sql: SELECT name FROM users; DROP TABLE users

cases.description: A single complex read with several joins is exactly what the gate must keep permitting — dangerous-op must not misfire on legitimate analytical SQL.
cases.sql: SELECT u.name, COUNT(t.id) FROM users u JOIN transactions t ON t.user_id = u.id JOIN merchants m ON m.id = t.merchant_id GROUP BY u.name
